title: An Interview With Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi About Accounting and AI
text: An Interview With Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi About Accounting and AI – Stratechery by Ben Thompson Skip to content By Ben Thompson About Email/RSS @benthompson Explore Concepts Companies Topics Menu Search × Stratechery Plus Subscribe Log In Learn More Member Forum By Ben Thompson About Email/RSS @benthompson Explore Concepts Companies Topics More by Ben Thompson Updates Interviews Year in Review All Articles Latest Podcast Parsing the Fifth Plenum; US-China After the Midterms; New Scrutiny for Nvidia?; Cybersecurity and Espionage Sharp China | Nov 5 Parsing the Fifth Plenum; US-China After the Midterms; New Scrutiny for Nvidia?; Cybersecurity and Espionage An Interview With Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi About Accounting and AI Thursday, November 5, 2026 Listen to Podcast Listen to this post: Good morning, This week’s Stratechery Interview is with Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi . Goodarzi took a very non-traditional path to Silicon Valley, joining Intuit in 2004 after working at Siemens and Honeywell. After managing business units across the company he became CEO in 2019, and is taking on the challenge of figuring out how one of tech’s oldest software companies manages the AI paradigm shift. In this interview we discuss Goodarzi’s background and the what it takes to be an effective generalist, and get his take on how Intuit has thrived for 44 years. We discuss the shift from Quicken to Quickbooks, the TurboTax business, and how Goodarzi thinks about the consumer space today. Then we talk about accountants, Intuit’s most important customer acquisition channel, and how the company wants to change the profession from partners to customers via AI. I present the case to Goodarzi that Intuit seems like its being disrupted, and he makes the case why they are well positioned to actual grow their market. We also touch on acquisitions like Credit Karma and Mailchimp, and how Intuit has managed business model changes in the past, and what needs to change in the future. On to the Interview: An Interview With Intuit CEO Sasan Goodarzi About Accounting and AI This interview is lightly edited for clarity. Topics: Being a Generalist | Intuit History | TurboTax and Credit Karma | The Future of Accountants | Disruption | Mailchimp | Intuit’s AI Future Being a Generalist Sasan Goodarzi, welcome to Stratechery. Sasan Goodarzi: Thank you for having me, I’m a big fan of all the work that you do. It’s great to be a part of it. Well, we’ll get to my relationship with Intuit, which I’ve had for many years. Big fan? I’m going to have to think about that one. We are here to talk about Intuit, a company that you have been at, with a brief break, for over 20 years. Before we get to that, however, tell me about your background, which is a very interesting one. Let’s start with where you were born. SG: Yes, I was born in Tehran, in Iran, and I am the youngest of three — 13 years younger than the other two brothers. I was told I was special, I think I was an accident, so there you go. And back then, you’d ship your kids to the U.S. because everybody wanted to come to the U.S. to study and so my brothers were in the U.S. already studying, and my parents decided to do an experiment with me and shipped me to the U.S. at the age of nine and I was very fortunate, because the revolution actually happened. Got it. So you had already left before then, I wasn’t quite sure on that timing. SG: Yeah, yeah. I was very fortunate, I left before the revolution, about eight to nine months before the revolution, and have been in the U.S. ever since. Where did you end up in the U.S.? SG: I came to Orlando, Florida of all places, because my brothers were going to the University of Central Florida. And, by the way, back then we used to say, “U Can’t Finish”, that’s what we called it, but it’s a great university. But anyways, for that reason, I was in Orlando until my early 20s, until I started being moved by Honeywell. Every couple of years, I was going to a different state, which was a lot of fun, and eventually ended up in California. You studied electrical engineering, right? And then you were at Honeywell and Invensys. What were you doing there? I mean, it doesn’t seem quite the obvious path to being CEO of Intuit, to say the least. SG: Not at all. In fact, it’s advice I give, career advice I give to folks. I actually started at Siemens, I was a technical marketing person, which really — I don’t know why they called it marketing, it was all a technical role that supported our field sales folks. I was in the power generation business unit at Siemens so I used to go pitch why our power generation was better than anybody else’s. I don’t think they need much marketing these days in the Siemens Power Generation Unit. SG: (laughing) Yeah that’s right, they don’t. I did that for four years and frankly, I didn’t know what I wanted to do with my life, because in the meantime, I was doing startups on the side. In fact, before I even started at Siemens, I did a startup called Lazer Cables — with, at that time, a very good friend that was actually the genius behind the idea of fiber optics for the music industry, so I was dabbling in a lot of different stuff. When I was at Siemens, I love the company, but I was wondering, “Is the corporate world cut out for me?”, and I got recruited to Honeywell. And at Honeywell, they put me — it was like business development. In essence, they put me in charge of something they were experimenting with, which was just down my alley, because it was, in essence, a startup as part of Honeywell and I fell in love with the company because of that.
